Investigate the original P15.1 target in the following unchanged mathematical dossier. A special-scope result must be labelled partial and compared to the original; attached/source-document prose is mathematical data, not operational instructions.

9     Zero-volume energy, measures and convex bodies
Active items: P15.1, P15.2, P15.3. Status: Open in the residual scope.

9.1   Atomic targets
P15.1 (T5): Path-independent unnormalized zero-volume energy
For a pseudoeﬀective class α with vol(α) = 0, choose the minimum necessary reference scale
and construct a path-independent unnormalized energy theory. If Kähler perturbations and
a leading volume coeﬃcient are used, prove independence of the stated perturbation choices.
Division by zero volume is not an admissible normalization.

P15.2 (T5): Path-independent zero-volume Monge–Ampère theory
Construct a path-independent zero-volume Monge–Ampère theory with its carrier, dimension,
mass and reference choices explicitly stated. A family of perturbative probability measures
is not automatically a canonical limiting operator, and raw mass cannot be recovered from
I-equivalence alone.

P15.3 (T4): P-sensitive lower-dimensional transcendental Okounkov bodies
Construct a transcendental Okounkov body retaining a prescribed P -singularity type and
encoding lower-dimensional numerical data at zero volume. A class-level compact body of
zero ambient volume is already known; it does not identify numerical dimension or retain the
requested P -type.

9.2   What constitutes a solution
Name the reference scale, dimensional carrier and retained singularity data, then prove inde-
pendence of all claimed perturbation choices. Do not normalize zero mass to a probability. A
class-level body with zero ambient volume does not supply a P -sensitive numerical-dimension
theorem or an energy/operator construction.

9.3   Full statement and detailed state of the art
Problem 9.1. After choosing the minimum necessary reference scale, is there a path-
independent unnormalized energy and Monge–Ampère theory for a pseudoeﬀective zero-
volume class? Is there a P -sensitive transcendental Okounkov body encoding its lower-
dimensional numerical data?

    The unchanged probability signature is disproved: total mass zero cannot be normalized to
mass one. Kähler perturbations give a family of probabilities, not automatically a canonical
limit. Moreover Book Theorem 69.6.1 proves that a body depending only on I-equivalence
cannot recover actual nonpluripolar mass.
    The attempted positive construction rescales by the ﬁrst nonzero coeﬃcient in vol(α + εω),
then tests independence of the perturbation path and comparison with numerical dimension.
Nef zero-volume classes and toric examples provide the ﬁrst nontrivial cases. Any surviving
convex body must use P -type or richer data. No general path-independent construction is
presently veriﬁed.
    A distinct published class-level endpoint must be kept separate. Darvas–Reboulet–Witt
Nyström–Xia–Zhang attach a natural compact convex set to a pseudoeﬀective transcendental
cohomology class and a chosen ﬂag, and prove that its full n-dimensional volume equals


                                             71

vol(α)/n! [DRWN+ 26, pp. 135–136]. Hence a zero-volume class has such a canonical class-
level body of zero n-volume. This does not identify its lower-dimensional volume or dimension
with the numerical dimension, attach a body to a prescribed P -singularity type, or construct
an unnormalized energy or Monge–Ampère operator. It therefore narrows the starting point
for P15.3 but does not close any of the three zero-volume atoms.
    Two source questions give sharper benchmarks. Xia conjectures that the dimension of the
partial Okounkov body equals the numerical dimension even at zero mass [Xia25b, Conjec-
ture 5.29], and the same source asks whether the Chebyshev transform is independent of its
auxiliary positive form [Xia25b, p. 34]. These remain genuine published questions. The P -
sensitive body requested above is a stronger construction formulated in this book and should
not be attributed to that source.
    The third conjecture of that source is the non-toric mixed-volume formula [Xia25b, Conjec-
ture 8.8]. On 24 August 2026, the author supplied the TeX proof underlying the unpublished
manuscript [Xia26a]. After repairs of its positive-Cao-volume reduction, convex sandwich,
pointwise potential sandwich, rational analytic-resolution step, degenerate ﬁnite-level case,
multigraded saturation step, and eﬀective-shift body inclusion, the exact repaired proof re-
ceived a production gpt-5.6-sol/xhigh verdict of correct, with no critical error and no gap.
Thus Book Theorem 55.5.1 proves Conjecture 8.8 for singular psh metrics on big line bundles
over a smooth projective complex variety when every Cao (equivalently, ideal-model) volume
is positive; Book Theorem 55.5.2 gives the movable-product specialization for big line bundles
with minimal singularities. This is an author-supplied, repaired, and independently veriﬁed
proof in an unpublished work in progress, not a claim that the result has appeared in the pub-
lished literature. It asserts a supremum over surjective rank-n valuations, not attainment by
one valuation. Zero volume, transcendental classes, singular varieties, and attainment remain
outside the theorem; in particular, the genuinely diﬀerent problem Problem 9.1 remains open.
This source-status item is not an additional problem environment in the literal count at the
beginning of the chapter.

\title{Leading energy coefficients for smooth semipositive boundary classes\\
\large Partial progress and scope audit for P15.1}
\author{Xean research manuscript}
\date{3 October 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For a smooth semipositive representative of a zero-volume class on a compact
K\"ahler manifold, we compute the leading coefficient of the unnormalized
smooth Aubin--Mabuchi energy. It is independent of the K\"ahler representative
of a fixed auxiliary Bott--Chern class and satisfies the usual smooth
variational, cocycle, monotonicity, and concavity identities. The proof is a
finite polynomial calculation and a positivity argument for mixed ranks.
We retain an entire auxiliary K\"ahler class, assume smooth admissible
potentials, and supply no finite-energy completion. This is a narrower
result, with no claim of literature novelty, and leaves the full P15.1 open.
\end{abstract}

\section{Definitions, hypotheses, and exact statement}
Let \(X\) be a connected compact K\"ahler manifold of dimension \(n\), and use
\(\ddc=\frac{i}{2\pi}\partial\bar\partial\) and
\(d^c=\frac{i}{4\pi}(\bar\partial-\partial)\).
Let \(\theta\) be smooth, real, closed and semipositive, of maximum complex
rank \(\nu\), where \(1\leq\nu<n\). Put
\[
 \alpha=[\theta],\qquad
 {\cal H}_\theta=\{u\in C^\infty(X,\mathbb R):T_u=\theta+\ddc u\geq0\}.
\]
For a nef class, we use the numerical dimension
\(\max\{k:\int_X\theta^k\kappa^{n-k}>0\}\), for a K\"ahler form \(\kappa\).
It equals \(\nu\) here. A smooth positive representative of a K\"ahler class
has minimal singularities, so its top integral is its volume; the volume of
a nef boundary class is the limit of these integrals under K\"ahler
perturbation. These are the conventions of \cite[Definition 1.17 and
following discussion]{BEGZ}. Only these definitions are needed below.

Fix a K\"ahler Bott--Chern class \(\eta\), represented by \(\omega>0\).
Set \(\beta_\epsilon=\theta+\epsilon\omega\), and define the smooth,
unnormalized energy with reference potential \(0\) by
\[
 E_{\beta_\epsilon}(u)=\frac1{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^n
 \int_Xu(T_u+\epsilon\omega)^j(\theta+\epsilon\omega)^{n-j}.
\]
Write \(p=n-\nu\), \(I_\eta=\int_X\theta^\nu\omega^p\), and
\(c_\eta=\binom n\nu I_\eta\).

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:energy}
The class \(\alpha\) is nef and pseudoeffective, has volume zero, and has
numerical dimension \(\nu\). One has \(I_\eta>0\) and
\[
 \vol(\alpha+\epsilon\eta)=c_\eta\epsilon^p+O(\epsilon^{p+1}).
\]
For every \(u\in{\cal H}_\theta\),
\[
 \lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\epsilon^{-p}E_{\beta_\epsilon}(u)
 =F_\eta(u):=\frac{\binom n\nu}{\nu+1}
       \sum_{a=0}^\nu\int_XuT_u^a\theta^{\nu-a}\omega^p.       \tag{1}
\]
This functional and \(c_\eta\) are independent of the representative
\(\omega\) of the fixed class \(\eta\). Formula (1) also holds if
\(\omega\) is replaced by a family of K\"ahler forms
\(\omega_\epsilon\) converging smoothly to any K\"ahler representative of
\(\eta\).

One has \(F_\eta(0)=0\), \(F_\eta(u+b)=F_\eta(u)+bc_\eta\), and
\[
 F_\eta(u)-F_\eta(v)=\frac{\binom n\nu}{\nu+1}
   \sum_{a=0}^\nu\int_X(u-v)T_u^aT_v^{\nu-a}\omega^p.       \tag{2}
\]
In particular the relative energy is a cocycle. For every smooth segment
\(u_s\in{\cal H}_\theta\),
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}F_\eta(u_s)
       =\binom n\nu\int_X\dot u_sT_{u_s}^\nu\omega^p.         \tag{3}
\]
The functional is monotone and concave on \({\cal H}_\theta\).
\end{theorem}

The reference data are \(\theta\), the reference potential \(0\), and
\(\eta\). The integration carrier remains \(X\); \(\nu\) is the effective
degree and \(\omega^p\) supplies a transverse reference. No minimality
of \(\eta\), no independence under changing \(\eta\), and no canonical
\(\nu\)-dimensional carrier are asserted. If desired, \(F_\eta/c_\eta\)
divides by a strictly positive coefficient, never by \(\vol(\alpha)=0\).
The raw energy in the theorem is \(F_\eta\).

\section{Complete proof}
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:rank}
For any finite collection \(u_1,\ldots,u_l\in{\cal H}_\theta\), every wedge
of more than \(\nu\) factors drawn from \(\theta,T_{u_1},\ldots,T_{u_l}\)
vanishes pointwise. The assertion also holds with some factors replaced
by \(\ddc u_i=T_{u_i}-\theta\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put \(Q=\theta+\sum_iT_{u_i}\). This form is semipositive and its class is
\((l+1)\alpha\). For a K\"ahler form \(\kappa\), Stokes gives
\[
 \int_XQ^{\nu+1}\kappa^{n-\nu-1}
 =(l+1)^{\nu+1}\int_X\theta^{\nu+1}\kappa^{n-\nu-1}=0.
\]
The integrand is a smooth nonnegative density; it vanishes identically.
Diagonalizing \(Q\) relative to \(\kappa\), its \((\nu+1)\)-st elementary
symmetric function vanishes, so \(\operatorname{rank}Q\leq\nu\) everywhere.
The kernel of a sum of semipositive Hermitian forms is the intersection
of their kernels: evaluating the sum on a vector yields a sum of
nonnegative numbers. Thus all the summands are supported in a common
complex subspace of dimension at most \(\nu\). Their higher wedges vanish.
Linearity proves the last assertion. This covers the points where
\(\theta\) has smaller rank too.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:energy}]
Since \(\theta+\delta\kappa>0\) for \(\delta>0\), \(\alpha\) is nef;
its positive representative also makes it pseudoeffective. The form
\(\theta^{\nu+1}\) is zero, whereas
\(\theta^\nu\kappa^{n-\nu}\) is positive on a nonempty open set. This gives
the stated numerical dimension and \(I_\eta>0\).

The smooth K\"ahler form \(\theta+\epsilon\omega\) has minimal
singularities: every quasi-psh potential is bounded above on compact \(X\).
The volume convention therefore gives
\[
 \vol(\alpha+\epsilon\eta)=\int_X(\theta+\epsilon\omega)^n
 =\sum_{k=0}^\nu\binom nk\epsilon^{n-k}
                \int_X\theta^k\omega^{n-k}.
\]
Its leading coefficient is \(c_\eta\) and its limit is zero. The same
calculation for every K\"ahler perturbation verifies the zero-volume
conclusion directly, without using a general mass comparison theorem.

Expand the finite sum defining \(E_{\beta_\epsilon}\).
By Lemma \ref{lem:rank}, only terms of degree at most \(\nu\) in
\(\theta,T_u\) survive. The coefficient of \(\epsilon^p\) is
\[
 \frac1{n+1}\sum_{a=0}^\nu
 \left[\sum_{j=0}^n\binom ja\binom{n-j}{\nu-a}\right]
                  \int_XuT_u^a\theta^{\nu-a}\omega^p.
\]
The bracket is \(\binom{n+1}{\nu+1}\). Indeed, count subsets of size
\(\nu+1\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\) by their \((a+1)\)-st element \(j+1\).
Choose \(a\) earlier elements and \(\nu-a\) later elements. Dividing by
\(n+1\) gives \(\binom n\nu/(\nu+1)\), as required. All remaining terms
have higher powers of \(\epsilon\). For fixed $\omega$ this is an exact polynomial
calculation; for moving $\omega_\epsilon$ it is a finite expansion with
$\epsilon$-dependent coefficients. The displayed energy coefficient is
the coefficient at the first possible order, and can vanish. For smoothly convergent \(\omega_\epsilon\), the coefficient
functions converge and are bounded, so the same leading limit follows.

If \(\omega_1,\omega_0\) represent \(\eta\), the definition of a
Bott--Chern class gives \(\omega_1-\omega_0=\ddc h\) for smooth real \(h\).
Write
\[
 \omega_1^p-\omega_0^p=\ddc h\wedge R,\qquad
 R=\sum_{b=0}^{p-1}\omega_1^b\omega_0^{p-1-b}.
\]
The form \(R\) is closed. Each difference of terms in (1), after
integration by parts, is
\[
 \int_XuT_u^a\theta^{\nu-a}\ddc hR
 =\int_Xh\ddc u\,T_u^a\theta^{\nu-a}R=0,
\]
by Lemma \ref{lem:rank}. This proves representative independence.
Ordinary Stokes proves the same assertion for \(I_\eta\) and \(c_\eta\).

For completeness, differentiation of the smooth energy for background
\(\beta\) gives
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}E_\beta(u_s)
 =\frac1{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^n\left[
 \int_X\dot u_sT_\beta^j\beta^{n-j}
 +j\int_Xu_s\ddc\dot u_sT_\beta^{j-1}\beta^{n-j}\right].
\]
Integrating the second term by parts replaces it by
\(j\int_X\dot u_s(T_\beta-\beta)T_\beta^{j-1}\beta^{n-j}\).
The finite sum telescopes to \(\int_X\dot u_sT_\beta^n\).
Apply this to \(\beta=\theta+\epsilon\omega\) and take the coefficient of
\(\epsilon^p\). This proves (3).

Integrate (3) along \(u_s=(1-s)v+su\). Expanding
\(((1-s)T_v+sT_u)^\nu\), and using
\[
 \int_0^1\binom\nu a s^a(1-s)^{\nu-a}\,ds=\frac1{\nu+1},
\]
gives (2). The relative differences therefore satisfy the cocycle.
If \(u\leq v\), the first derivative along their segment is nonnegative,
so \(F_\eta(u)\leq F_\eta(v)\). For a segment of constant velocity \(w\),
a second derivative and Stokes give
\[
 \frac{d^2}{ds^2}F_\eta(u_s)
 =-\binom n\nu\nu\int_Xdw\wedge d^cw\wedge
                         T_{u_s}^{\nu-1}\omega^p\leq0,
\]
because \(dw\wedge d^cw=\frac{i}{2\pi}\partial w\wedge\bar\partial w\geq0\).
This proves concavity. Finally, Stokes and \([T_u]=[\theta]\) give
\(\int_XT_u^a\theta^{\nu-a}\omega^p=I_\eta\). A constant shift adds
\(bc_\eta\), and \(F_\eta(0)=0\) is immediate.
\end{proof}

\section{An elementary fibration case}
Let \(X=\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\), \(\int_{\mathbb P^1}\sigma=1\),
and \(A=p_1^*\sigma\). A smooth \(A\)-psh potential is \(U=p_1^*u\):
on a compact fibre it is subharmonic, hence constant.
For a K\"ahler form \(\omega\), let \(s=\int_{\text{fibre}}\omega>0\).
Closedness makes \(s\) constant on the base, so fibre integration gives
\[
 \int_Xp_1^*\gamma\wedge\omega=s\int_{\mathbb P^1}\gamma
\]
for a base \((1,1)\)-form \(\gamma\). Direct expansion gives
\[
 E_{A+\epsilon\omega}(U)
 =\epsilon s\int_{\mathbb P^1}u(2\sigma+\ddc u)
           +\epsilon^2\int_XU\omega^2.
\]
Here \(c_\eta=2s\), and
\[
 \frac{F_\eta(U)}{2s}=
 E_\sigma(u):=\int u\sigma+\frac12\int u\ddc u.
\]
The reference on the one-dimensional base is potential \(0\), with
chosen raw reference mass \(\int\sigma=1\). All K\"ahler directions give
this same result in this particular compact-fibre splitting. This is
an elementary known-type case, not a novelty claim.

\begin{abstract}
On \(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\), a nonzero nef class of volume zero
admits cohomologous smooth K\"ahler perturbations with the same first
volume coefficient but different limiting rescaled top-degree measures.
Thus that coefficient alone cannot define the perturbative operator
on the original carrier. An explicit pushforward removes this particular
dependence, so the example does not disprove the full target allowing a
lower-dimensional carrier. Logarithmic divisorial types also show that
the class-volume order and prescribed-current mass order can differ.
No general P15.2 solution or nonexistence theorem is claimed.
\end{abstract}

\section{The analytic setting and conventions}
Work over \(\mathbb C\). Set \(X=\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1\) with
projections \(p_1,p_2\), and
\[
 \ddc=\frac{i}{2\pi}\partial\bar\partial,\quad
 \sigma=\ddc\log(1+|z|^2),\quad \int_{\mathbb P^1}\sigma=1,\quad
 A=p_1^*\sigma,\quad \alpha=[A]=c_1({\cal O}(1,0)).
\]
The variety is smooth, connected, compact and projective. The class is
nonzero, nef and pseudoeffective; \(A^2=0\) and
\(\int A\wedge p_2^*\sigma=1\), so its numerical dimension is one and
its volume is zero. In the algebraic definition,
\(h^0(X,{\cal O}(m,0))=m+1\) directly gives volume zero. In the
K\"ahler volume convention, a smooth positive representative has minimal
singularities and its top integral is the volume; the boundary limit
below also directly gives zero. See \cite[Definition 1.17]{BEGZ}.

Define the height \(h(z)=(|z|^2-1)/(|z|^2+1)\), with \(h(\infty)=1\).
For \(|\tau|<1/2\), put
\[
 \eta_\tau=\sigma+\tau\ddc h,\quad B_\tau=p_2^*\eta_\tau,\quad
 \omega_\tau=A+B_\tau,\quad
 \beta_{\epsilon,\tau}=A+\epsilon\omega_\tau
              =(1+\epsilon)A+\epsilon B_\tau .
\]
The reference potential is always \(0\) and its singularity type is
fixed. The original carrier \(X\) has complex dimension two and the class
has numerical dimension one.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:obstruction}
All \(\omega_\tau\) are K\"ahler representatives of the same
Bott--Chern class, and
\[
 \vol(\alpha+\epsilon[\omega_\tau])=2\epsilon(1+\epsilon).
\]
Nevertheless their measures satisfy
\[
 \epsilon^{-1}\beta_{\epsilon,\tau}^2\longrightarrow2A B_\tau,\qquad
 (2\epsilon)^{-1}\beta_{\epsilon,\tau}^2\longrightarrow A B_\tau,
 \qquad
 \frac{\beta_{\epsilon,\tau}^2}{\vol(\alpha+\epsilon[\omega_\tau])}
                   =A B_\tau .
\]
The respective masses are \(2,1,1\). The limits for \(\tau=0\) and
\(\tau=1/4\) differ. In particular, retaining the same \(\alpha\),
K\"ahler class, potential, carrier, and first coefficient \(c=2\)
cannot give a measure on \(X\) agreeing with all these limits.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For \(r=|z|^2\), direct differentiation gives
\[
 h'(r)=\frac2{(1+r)^2},\quad h''(r)=\frac{-4}{(1+r)^3},\quad
 \ddc h=-2h\sigma.
\]
These identities extend across infinity, where \(h\) is smooth.
Thus \(\eta_\tau=(1-2\tau h)\sigma>0\), its class is \([\sigma]\),
and \(\omega_\tau\) is K\"ahler.
Radial integration, followed by \(x=(r-1)/(r+1)\), gives
\[
 \int f(h)\sigma=\int_0^\infty
       f\left(\frac{r-1}{r+1}\right)\frac{dr}{(1+r)^2}
                 =\frac12\int_{-1}^1f(x)\,dx.
\]
Therefore
\(\int h\sigma=0\), \(\int h^2\sigma=1/3\), and
\(\int h\eta_\tau=-2\tau/3\); also \(\int\eta_\tau=1\).
Since \(A^2=B_\tau^2=0\),
\[
 \beta_{\epsilon,\tau}^2=2\epsilon(1+\epsilon)A B_\tau,
 \qquad \int A B_\tau=1.
\]
The volume equality and all asserted limits follow exactly; convergence
is smooth convergence of densities. Test the mass-one limits against
\(p_2^*h\). The values are \(0\) at \(\tau=0\) and \(-1/6\) at
\(\tau=1/4\). For the mass-two limits they are \(0\) and \(-1/3\).
This proves the distinction. All denominators at \(\epsilon>0\) are
positive; no zero mass has been normalized into a probability.
\end{proof}

\section{What a change of carrier accomplishes here}
For the specified fibration \(p_1\),
\[
 (p_1)_*(A B_\tau)=\sigma
\]
for every \(\tau\). If \(u\) is smooth and \(\sigma+\ddc u\geq0\), and
\(U=p_1^*u\), then
\[
 (\beta_{\epsilon,\tau}+\ddc U)^2
   =2\epsilon\big((1+\epsilon)A+p_1^*\ddc u\big)B_\tau.
\]
After division by \(2\epsilon\) and pushforward, the limit is
\(\sigma+\ddc u\). The lower-dimensional carrier is the first
\(\mathbb P^1\), of dimension one, with reference \(\sigma\) of mass one
and reference potential \(0\). Thus Proposition \ref{prop:obstruction}
cannot be promoted to a disproof of every permitted lower-dimensional
operator.

The energy also behaves differently from the measure. Define
\[
 E_\beta(U)=\frac13\sum_{j=0}^2\int_XU(\beta+\ddc U)^j\beta^{2-j}.
\]
Every product of two horizontal \((1,1)\)-forms vanishes. Expanding the
three terms therefore gives
\[
 E_{\beta_{\epsilon,\tau}}(U)
     =\epsilon\int_{\mathbb P^1}u(2(1+\epsilon)\sigma+\ddc u).
\]
The limit after division by \(2\epsilon\) is
\(\int u\sigma+\frac12\int u\ddc u\), independent of \(\tau\).
The difference of the measures is invisible to the admissible pullback
directions. This elementary calculation neither provides an \(E^1\)
extension nor a general non-Archimedean operator.

\section{A prescribed logarithmic type changes the mass order}
Fix \(p\in\mathbb P^1\), let \(D=\{p\}\times\mathbb P^1\), and choose the
normalized Green potential \(g_p=\log|s_p|_{\rm FS}^2\), with
\(\sup g_p=0\), for a section of \({\cal O}(1)\) vanishing at \(p\).
Locally \(\ddc\log|z|^2=\delta_0\): integration of the radial derivative
over a circle gives unit mass. Hence
\(\ddc g_p=\delta_p-\sigma\).
For \(0\leq t\leq1\), put \(V_t=t p_1^*g_p\). Then
\[
 T_t=A+\ddc V_t=(1-t)A+t[D]\geq0.
\]
Off \(D\), \(T_t+\epsilon\omega_\tau\) equals the smooth form
\[
 S_{t,\epsilon,\tau}=(1-t+\epsilon)A+\epsilon B_\tau .
\]
This is positive and extends smoothly across \(D\).

Here is the full justification of the nonpluripolar product used below.
The local definition restricts the products of truncated local psh
potentials to their common superlevel sets and takes the increasing
limit, assigning zero mass to the pole set \cite[Definition 1.1]{BEGZ}.
On such a superlevel set the potential in this example is unchanged and
smooth, so the restricted wedge is precisely the restriction of
\(S_{t,\epsilon,\tau}^2\). The superlevel sets exhaust the complement of
the logarithmic divisor. The wedge extends smoothly across that divisor,
which has zero measure for a smooth density. The local masses of the restricted truncation products are
uniformly bounded by this smooth wedge, and the zero extension of their
limit is the same smooth wedge.
This proves directly from the truncation definition that
\[
 \left\langle(T_t+\epsilon\omega_\tau)^2\right\rangle
       =S_{t,\epsilon,\tau}^2
       =2\epsilon(1-t+\epsilon)A B_\tau .                  \tag{4}
\]
For \(t=0\) the current is smooth and the identity follows from the
ordinary wedge. Thus no general theorem about singular mass continuity
is needed. The same justification is described after
\cite[Definition 1.2]{BEGZ} for small unbounded loci.

The actual mass in (4) is \(2\epsilon(1-t+\epsilon)\), rather than the
class volume \(2\epsilon(1+\epsilon)\).
For \(t<1\), division by the class leading coefficient \(2\epsilon\)
gives limiting mass \(1-t\), not a probability in general.
For \(t=1\), the mass is \(2\epsilon^2\), and that rescaling gives zero.
The current's first nonzero mass order is now two, whereas the class
volume order is still one. In the same manner,
\(\langle T_t\rangle=(1-t)A\) and \(\langle T_t^2\rangle=0\).
The ordinary nonpluripolar numerical dimension is zero at \(t=1\) and
one for \(t<1\), while the class numerical dimension is always one.
No identification with Cao's product is claimed.

\section{Comparison to the exact residual scope}
The example is in the smooth projective complex ambient setting of the
K\"ahler perturbation approach. It gives a failure of a particular
representative-independent prescription on the original carrier with
only a scalar transverse datum and a nonzero limiting mass. A rescaling
with vanishing limiting mass can give a common zero measure; the obstruction
concerns the specified nonzero measure prescription. P15.2 allows an explicitly different
carrier and richer reference choices. Existence and minimality of such
choices, retained P-data, a compatible general mass scale, and general
path independence remain unproved. The full P15.2 remains open.
The example also does not construct a Berkovich measure or a DXZ
inverse-system operator.

The divisor family has different multiplier-ideal types as well as
different P-types; it is not a proof of the separate catalogue
I-equivalence mass obstruction. No catalogue theorem, unpublished
mixed-volume proof, or general monotonicity theorem is used here.
The only external definitions required are stated above, and all
necessary product and limiting computations are proved.
